item.title: WASC restores accreditation for Guam schools after purchase order problem resolved
item.description: The Western Association of Schools and Colleges has restored full accreditation for Guam schools, following an announcement earlier this week that accreditation had been terminated. Guam Department of Education spokesperson Damen Michael Borja said that termination stemmed from an outstanding purchase order payment from the 2024-25 school year.
item.content:encoded:
The Western Association of Schools and Colleges has restored full accreditation for Guam schools, following an announcement earlier this week that accreditation had been terminated.

Guam Department of Education spokesperson Damen Michael Borja said that termination stemmed from an outstanding purchase order payment from the 2024-25 school year.

GDOE officials worked with WASC and took care of the payment on Monday.

"We inherited this issue, and we took it on directly by reviewing the invoices, correcting the billing errors, and staying in constant communication with WASC,” Superintendent Judith Won Pat stated in a news release. “I'm grateful for their confirmation that our accreditation is continuous, and our focus remains on making sure our schools and students are never adversely affected."

In written confirmation to the department, WASC stated that there was no break in membership in good standing and that accreditation is considered continuous.

All GDOE schools remain accredited through school year 2029.

item.title: Police, AG investigating death of murder suspect Nicholas Wayne Moore
item.description: The Guam Police Department and the Office of the Attorney General are asking for information from the public as they investigate the death of murder suspect Nicholas Wayne Moore. Moore’s attorney, Mike Phillips, issued a statement Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Police Department and the Office of the Attorney General are asking for information from the public as they investigate the death of murder suspect Nicholas Wayne Moore.

Moore’s attorney, Mike Phillips, issued a statement Wednesday.

“Nicholas was found early this morning in his bedroom. It was clear at that time Nicholas passed away. At this time his passing is being investigated and the cause of death remains unknown,” Phillips said.

He said the family is working with investigators.

Moore was charged in the 2020 killing of Michael Jose Castro, whose car was found in the compound of Unitek Environmental, a company run by Moore’s father.

Moore was also charged in a separate 2020 Agana Heights shooting that sent a man to the hospital. After numerous delays, a mistrial was declared in that case in 2023.

He had also been indicted in a criminal sexual conduct case involving a girl under the age of 16.

“We are shocked by Nicholas’ passing and just met with him yesterday,” Phillips said. “We mourn Nicholas’ passing and look forward to receiving information regarding the cause of death.”

On Wednesday, police and Attorney General Douglas Moylan issued a statement saying they were investigating the circumstances surrounding the death.

“Because this remains an active investigation, authorities are limiting the release of additional information at this time to protect the integrity of the investigation,” the statement said. “We specifically ask that anyone who has information as to the circumstances leading up to Mr. Nicholas Moore’s untimely death please come forward to speak with a GPD Criminal Investigation Division detective.”

Police can be reached at (671) 475-8615/6/7, or tips can be anonymously submitted online with Guam Crime Stoppers at www.guamcrimestoppers.com .

item.title: Crime Stoppers tips lead DPS to identify Airport Road Jane Doe

item.content:encoded:
The woman whose decomposed body was found near a farm off Airport Road in July has been identified as Maria Edna Clarin, 48, of Afetna, according to the Department of Public Safety.

DPS public information officer Fred Sato said Tuesday that investigators confirmed Clarin’s identity after verifying Crime Stoppers tips and conducting multiple interviews. A family member later identified her, ending the two‑month effort to determine who the woman was.

Clarin’s body was discovered at about 9:47 a.m. July 20 by a resident searching for a missing cow along the western boundary of his family’s compound. The resident noticed a fresh trail through tall grass and followed it into a jungle area between two neighboring properties, where he found what appeared to be a deceased person and immediately contacted authorities.

An autopsy conducted by Dr. Philip Dauterman found no evidence of foul play, according to DPS.

Investigators said there were no defensive wounds, no physical trauma, and no ligature marks around the neck. Toxicology tests were also negative. Because of the condition of the remains, the cause and manner of death remain undetermined.

DPS said the investigation is continuing and additional information will be released as it becomes available.

item.title: An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot
item.description: For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter. Fall has only just begun, but it's already time to start thinking about the quintessential winter bug: the flu .
item.content:encoded:
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Fall has only just begun, but it's already time to start thinking about the quintessential winter bug: the flu .

The annual flu season usually starts in October or November. But this year, it looks like the flu started to pick up in early September.

"There are enough signs pointing in the same direction to make me think, 'OK, yes. This is the start of flu season,'" says Caitlin Rivers , an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

The percentage of people testing positive for the flu in the West has been rising steadily since around the beginning of September, she says. And the number of people showing up in emergency departments because of the flu has also been rising for weeks, she adds.

"It's very uncommon to see flu activity rising this early. It's activity that we might normally see more like November or December," she says.

The timing of the flu season isn't the only thing that's odd. It's also unusual that flu activity seems to have started in Western states, such as California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska.

"It typically starts in the South and then expands from there," Rivers says. "So two uncommon developments there."

Rivers stresses that the amount of flu activity is still very low in most parts of the country. But that's starting to change as the flu picks up nationwide.

It's unclear why flu activity would have started so early, and in such an unusual part of the country. But one clue might be a new variant that evolved a mutation, which appears to make it better at evading existing immunity, especially among teenagers.

"That's our best argument for what's going on right now in terms of this early flu season," says Dr. Alex Greninger , a virologist who heads infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington. Doctors there are seeing as much flu right now as they usually would around Christmas, and the mutated variant appears to be common, he says.

So Greninger, Rivers and others are urging people to think about getting their flu shot earlier than usual.

"It's crucial that people get an influenza vaccine," says Scott Hensley , a virologist at the University of Pennsylvania. "And this might be a year that people might want to get a vaccine early."

But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn't been promoting flu shots as it usually does. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who oversees the CDC, is a long-time vaccine skeptic.

"It is disappointing that CDC is quiet given that flu kills of hundreds of kids a year and can result in tens of thousands of hospitalizations and tens of thousands of deaths," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis , who resigned last year as the director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest what he called political interference at the agency.

The CDC declined to make an official available to NPR for this story. In a statement, a CDC spokesperson said, "CDC is developing a communications strategy to provide clear, accessible information about influenza vaccination and other critical steps people can take to protect themselves during respiratory virus season. This includes information about the benefits and risks of vaccination to support informed decision-making."

item.title: 'Medicare for All' message attracts midterm voters buckling under medical bills
item.description: Christina Starks-Clay doesn't know how "Medicare for All" would work exactly, but she's willing to bet it'd be better than what she has now. While standing in line for a Sept. 11 town hall for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Lansing, she whipped out her phone and pulled up a screenshot.
item.content:encoded:
Christina Starks-Clay doesn't know how "Medicare for All" would work exactly, but she's willing to bet it'd be better than what she has now.

While standing in line for a Sept. 11 town hall for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Lansing, she whipped out her phone and pulled up a screenshot.

It was of the $1,000 cashier's check she'd picked up at the bank that day to pay down a chunk of her son's dental bills.

Starks-Clay, an early childhood special education paraprofessional, still owed the dentist $389, even with good dental insurance. Her own cleaning a few weeks before had cost $600.

She tried to talk herself down at the bank, to focus on being grateful for what she could afford.

"I'm like, 'Tina, OK, you were in a position for this moment to do this,'" she said. "A lot of people couldn't do what I had to do today. I couldn't do it. But I did it. So I need to hear, how are you going to make this better for everyone?"

Many who waited in the hot sun that afternoon in a line stretching blocks through downtown Lansing shared similar anxieties.

A man ahead of Starks-Clay talked about watching his brother rack up thousands of dollars in medical debt.

A professor emeritus at nearby Michigan State University worried aloud about his grandkids' medical care, because his adult kids were struggling to meet a $9,000 insurance deductible.

Healthcare workers who'd turned up for the event described patients choosing between affording medication or food, or how they themselves had been financially devastated by a medical crisis.

They all knew El-Sayed's rallying cry by heart, chanting it when the Michigan Democrat took the stage: "Money out of politics! Money in your pocket! Medicare for All!"

Support for Medicare for All is at its highest in at least a decade, according to a new KFF poll. The survey found two-thirds of Americans now favor expanding the government health program that largely covers seniors (about half of whom are enrolled in private plans through Medicare Advantage).

But many people don't actually know how to define Medicare for All. Traditionally, the idea has been to establish a single health insurance program, run by the federal government, that would guarantee coverage for Americans and minimize or even eliminate private insurance. How much people like the idea depends on what they're told about it, pollsters have found.

Still, at a time when fewer than half of Americans say they can afford their healthcare, Medicare for All has become a progressive shorthand for radical, systemic change.

"Too many people don't have health insurance, too many people who do have insurance can't afford medical care, and many people are terrified about the costs of being sick," said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who specializes in the politics of healthcare reform.

"And in an electorate that wants change, that is disenchanted with the status quo, Medicare for All is an important symbol," he said.

That's why Democrats running for Senate seats in the midterm elections in such states as Maine, Minnesota, and Florida tout their support for scrapping the current health insurance system in favor of broad Medicare coverage. But nowhere is the issue as central to a race as in Michigan, where Medicare for All has become synonymous with El-Sayed.

El-Sayed, who trained as a doctor and served as Detroit's top public health official, has campaigned on Medicare for All since his unsuccessful bid for governor in 2018. To Starks-Clay, that means he has a plan and will "stick to it," she said.

That's appealing to voters right now, said Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.

"When we ask people what do they want to hear from candidates in regards to healthcare, it's a plan to bring down healthcare costs," Kirzinger said.

Medicare for All has been the shiny object of progressive politics in previous campaigns, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 presidential bid and the 2020 Democratic presidential primary. Its popularity rises and falls in cycles, Oberlander said. And today, people are painfully aware their care is getting more expensive and harder to access.

In the first decade or so after the passage of the Affordable Care Act in 2010, the nation's uninsured rate was cut nearly in half . Insurance companies could no longer deny people coverage based on preexisting conditions. Since then, to cover more people, 40 states plus Washington, D.C., have expanded Medicaid, the government health program for those with low incomes or disabilities.

Now it feels as if we're moving backward, Oberlander said. "We are now, in the past two years, in an era where the Trump administration and congressional Republicans have reversed that progress."

Michigan, a battleground state that President Donald Trump won in 2024, saw some of the steepest ACA plan enrollment drops after the GOP-controlled Congress allowed enhanced tax subsidies, which helped people afford their premiums, to expire at the end of last year.

Insurance companies in Michigan hiked individual marketplace rates by an average of 20%.

And up to 355,000 Michiganders are expected to lose their Medicaid coverage in 2028 because of cuts included in Trump's signature law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to estimates from the Urban Institute , a left-leaning think tank.

At El-Sayed's town hall in Lansing, Darleana Ash said patients at the medical diagnostics lab where she works are increasingly skipping tests because they can't afford them.

Others drive hours from rural areas because their local labs have closed or are no longer in their insurance networks. She worries about the patients who must choose between their medications and groceries some months.

"If you got somebody that's 75, 80 years old, guess what? They're going to go without the medication, because they got to eat," she said.

Packed in near the front of the crowded town hall was Cindy Lou Coolich, a boisterous retiree wearing a campaign T-shirt and cowboy hat.

item.title: 5 things civil rights data says about public schools
item.description: Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly. The number of kids in preschool rose in the 2023-24 school year, while those in K-12 public schools declined. The population of students with disabilities grew. Black students were more likely to be suspended than students of other races. And the teacher workforce was far less diverse than the student population.
item.content:encoded:
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

The number of kids in preschool rose in the 2023-24 school year, while those in K-12 public schools declined. The population of students with disabilities grew. Black students were more likely to be suspended than students of other races. And the teacher workforce was far less diverse than the student population.

All of this information comes from the latest Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC): a federal survey that paints one of the most comprehensive pictures of how American students are being treated at school. The federal government has been gathering this kind of information for over 50 years, partly to help the U.S. Education Department hold schools accountable for protecting student civil rights.

The Trump administration published the latest CRDC from the 2023-24 school year six months later than promised. When it finally did share the information on Aug. 31, collected from over 97,000 public schools, it was without a usual "First Look Report" that makes the information easier to understand for the public. Now, that too , is available.

The findings are about 49.7 million public school students and include data on enrollment, harassment and the treatment of students with disabilities, among other things. But one group was left out: nonbinary students. While data on nonbinary students was collected under the Biden administration, the Trump administration chose to withhold it from the public release.

Maithreyi Gopalan of the University of Oregon, who helps lead the research and policy group AdvancED Equity , and Dan Losen of the National Center for Youth Law, both independently analyzed the data and shared some of what they learned with NPR.

Here are five things they found striking:

Some 1.5 million children were enrolled in public preschool programs — a 12% jump from the 2021-22 school year, but still slightly lower than 2019 . "It's part recovery, part expansion," says Gopalan. By recovery, she means the number of preschoolers started rising again from a pandemic low. By expansion, Gopalan is referring to the fact that some states are investing more in early childhood education, which may account for some of the increases.

According to the National Institute for Early Education Research , state-funded pre-K enrollment rose nearly 15% between 2021-22 and 2023-24. For example, in 2023-24, California was in its second year of expanding its universal transitional kindergarten (TK) program for 4-year-olds, and the state enrolled nearly 36,000 more children in preschool or TK than the year before. Colorado and New Mexico are among other states that are rapidly expanding preschool access.

At the same time, K-12 enrollment fell almost 1% compared with the 2021-22 school year. The decrease is consistent with other data and could have to do with declining birthrates and an increase in private school and homeschooled students in some states, Gopalan says.

The number of students who were suspended increased across the board: 2.5 million students were punished with one or more out-of-school suspensions while 2.3 million students faced in-school suspensions in 2023-24. That's up by about 100,000 students in each category compared with the last report from 2021-22. Notably, nearly 7 out of 10 public schools reported an increase in students seeking mental health services since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, according to other federal data .

While the increase in suspensions may seem modest, Losen says it shows that the pattern of keeping children out of school as punishment is still widespread in America's public schools. His research shows that most districts suspend students for what he calls minor offenses rather than unsafe behavior.

"It could be truancy, it could be repeated tardiness, dress code violations." Those missed days of school mean missed days of learning: Losen's research shows that about a decade ago, students were losing out on 11 million days of school because of suspensions. According to the latest CRDC, he says they missed over 14 million days in the 2023-24 school year.

"That lost instruction time matters more than people realize," he says. "Even one out-of-school suspension greatly increases the risk of dropping out of a school or winding up in the juvenile justice system."

He adds that suspensions are often an ineffective way to change behavior and that there are more constructive ways to help students, including with emotional support and better training for teachers.

Another persistent pattern with school discipline is who faces it: Losen says the latest data show that Black students lost over four times as many days of school compared to white peers because of out-of-school suspension.

The CRDC reinforces what other national data shows: The population of students with disabilities is on the rise, and boys make up a much bigger share than girls — nearly two-thirds — of these students. While the previous CRDC showed 17% of students had disabilities, the newest data show they made up 19% of all students enrolled in public schools. And they were suspended out of school at disproportionately high rates.

Losen says the lost days of school for these students don't just mean they're missing learning, it also means they may be losing out on key services they get during school, such as mental health counseling or physical therapy.

Disabled students are also among the least likely groups to be enrolled in Advanced Placement (AP) classes in high school. Losen says that's a longstanding pattern, in part, because of assumptions that they can't achieve at high levels. AP classes might not be the right fit for some students with intellectual disabilities, he says, but many students have disabilities that have little to do with their academic potential.

And Gopalan says these classes don't just represent how much rigor students are exposed to. "These are all gateways to college, other opportunities beyond high school. And we see gaps in opportunity and access for students with disabilities."

For the first time since the 1970s, the latest CRDC gathered information about teachers' race, ethnicity and sex. It found that the workforce is 75% white, 9% Black and 11% Latino — a drastically different makeup than the students they serve.

Gopalan says the data is valuable partly because teacher diversity can play a role in student success. For example, she says some research shows that "Black students have better achievement, better school discipline outcomes, and a whole host of other outcomes when they're taught by Black teachers." And studies show that having more Black or Latino teachers can help all students.

This collection also captures the qualifications of teachers. "Research shows that access to certified and experienced teachers and to counselors has a positive effect on who finishes high school, who graduates, and who goes on to colleges," Gopalan says. Yet, more than 720,000 students go to schools where fewer than half of teachers met state certification requirements, and Black and Latino students make up 73% of those students.

Under President Joe Biden, the CRDC required schools to report the experiences of nonbinary students for the first time. The information was collected for the 2023-24 school year, but the Trump administration chose not to release it, citing an executive order that called for the federal government to "recognize two sexes, male and female."

"There is no Civil Rights Data Collection where they intentionally collected data and then just suppressed it," says Losen, who has been analyzing the CRDC for more than 25 years. He says students who are nonbinary are more likely to face difficulties like bullying at school. "Whatever kinds of injustices they're experiencing, we would start to see that it was beginning to be reflected in those data, and now we can't see it." According to one UCLA analysis , about 3% of children ages 13 to 17 identify as transgender nationwide, which includes nonbinary youth.

In an emailed statement, the Education Department did not answer NPR's questions about its decision to withhold data on nonbinary students, instead highlighting the Trump administration's priority to collect data about sexual offenses on school campuses.

Data for the next CRDC is being collected for the 2025-26 school year, according to the Department. While much of the survey will remain the same, all questions about nonbinary students have been removed from the list. Questions related to whether students are harassed or bullied on the basis of gender identity will also be removed.

Edited by Nirvi Shah Graphics by Rahul Mukherjee Visual design by LA Johnson

item.title: 3 years on, Israelis grapple with reports Netanyahu was warned before Oct. 7 attacks
item.description: TEL AVIV, Israel — As Israel marks three years since Hamas launched its surprise Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack. item.content:encoded:
TEL AVIV, Israel — As Israel marks three years since Hamas launched its surprise Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally warned about a potential Hamas attack, and his security agencies were notified repeatedly, in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023, four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR.

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz , The New York Times and The Atlantic first reported about the warnings.

Netanyahu has denied he was warned, calling the reports "fake news" and filing a defamation lawsuit last week against Israeli news outlets that published them. He and his defense minister have issued new warnings that Hamas could try to attack or "challenge" Israel on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to national elections later this month.

But the Oct. 7, 2023, security failure — as well as Netanyahu's repeated refusal to take responsibility for it — has become a lightning rod in Israel as the prime minister seeks a new term in national elections this month.

"You didn't protect my son," yelled out one bereaved Israeli father whose son was killed in the Hamas-led attack, as the prime minister spoke at a memorial ceremony this week for the victims.

One warning came directly from the leader of Hamas in Gaza weeks before Oct. 7, a Palestinian mediator told NPR and other media outlets.

Former Palestinian Authority official Sufian Abu Zaida said he helped mediate secret Hamas-Israel talks for more than a year leading up to Oct. 7. He said Hamas wanted Israel to release Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and offered in exchange to release two living Israeli hostages and the bodies of two Israeli soldiers held in Gaza for years. But he said Israel was unwilling to release as many prisoners as Hamas had demanded.

On Sept. 14, 2023, Abu Zaida said, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar dictated a message for him to deliver to Israel: "By the end of September, we will put cards on the table. There will be an earthquake in the negotiations, and the Israelis should prepare to empty their prisons."

He did not know what kind of earthquake Sinwar meant, but he said he sent the message to an Israeli intelligence official who acknowledged receiving it and to Mohammed Dahlan, a Palestinian confidant of the leader of the United Arab Emirates.

"What happened [on] the 7th of October is needless," Abu Zaida told NPR.

Days before the Oct. 7 attacks, the leader of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, called Netanyahu and told him that Hamas' leader in Gaza was planning a big assault against Israel, according to a person close to Dahlan. Dahlan was the Palestinian Authority's head of security in Gaza before Hamas seized control of the territory in 2007.

The Emirati leader told Netanyahu in a phone call that lasted more than 40 minutes that a "quake" would hit the region if no progress was achieved regarding a prisoner deal between Hamas and Israel, the person said.

The person spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the call. The phone call was previously reported by Haaretz and The New York Times .

The UAE did not deny the report, saying only that it maintained dialogue with Israel.

A senior Egyptian official told NPR that Egypt had specific intelligence about Hamas movements and that Egypt's head of intelligence at the time, Abbas Kamel, had traveled to Israel with two other senior officials and met with Israel's Mossad and Shin Bet intelligence chiefs.

The official said Kamel relayed a warning that Gaza was on the verge of an "explosion" because of Israel's blockade, the condition of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and concerns that Israel might move to annex the occupied West Bank.

The official was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. The Atlantic reported that Kamel's visit to Israel was on Sept 26.

Nimrod Novik, a fellow at the Israel Policy Forum think tank and a former top adviser to late Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres, told NPR that he was informed before Oct. 7 by a person with firsthand knowledge that Egypt had delivered warnings to several senior Israeli officials that "Gaza is about to explode in your face."

Novik said one warning was an "urgent and dramatic message" from Egypt, delivered to a person close to Netanyahu some 10 days prior to Oct. 7.

"I'm certain that the issue of the early warnings on October 7 is going to continue to play with heightened emotions as we approach Election Day," said Novik. "This is going to be an indictment for history, not just for the elections."

Netanyahu has blamed Israeli security organizations for failing to stop the Oct. 7 attacks. He and his government have yet to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the failures around Oct. 7, despite public demand.

The new reports about warnings issued to Israel "actually turn the story on its head," pointing the finger right back at the prime minister, said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

"It violates the basic narrative that Netanyahu tries to tell Israelis," said Talshir.

NPR's Aya Batrawy contributed to this report.
